title: God Answers the Righteous at Once
english: … brightness benefits in no small measure those who look on them. Indeed, Christ said to the holy apostles: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). So we shall be radiant, with the glory from God moving all around us and, as it were, clothing us, the glory he would grant to those who devote themselves to righteousness.

When these things are yours, he says, then you will cry out, and God will hear you; while you are still speaking he will say, “Here I am” (Isaiah 58:9). For “he listens to the prayers of the righteous” (Proverbs 15:29), as it is written. And as the Psalmist says: “The eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayer” (Psalm 34:15).

Because he is good, he will grant the requests of those who ask, but not to all at once. To those who have excelled in righteousness, however, he holds out what they ask without any delay and lends them a most ready ear, so that over each of their requests they say with joy: “He heard my voice from his holy temple, and my cry before him will come into his ears” (Psalm 18:6). So the cry “Here I am,” while the righteous man is still speaking and lifting up his prayers, shows plainly the generosity that will not delay and the great readiness of God who gives.

“If you take away from yourself the bond, and the stretching out of the hand, and the word of grumbling, and give your bread to the hungry, and satisfy the humbled soul, then your light will rise in the darkness, and your darkness will be as noon, and your God will be with you always” (Isaiah 58:9–11).

The choicest lessons, even if people hear them many times, still bring benefit. So the all-wise Paul writes to those who believed through him: “To say the same things to you is no trouble to me, and for you it is safe” (Philippians 3:1). So in many ways he comes to us saying the same things, making plain the roads to good standing and describing the splendor of the rewards to be given to the saints. He does this to make them still more eager to choose to do the things by which they would become worthy of honor and would find the generosity that comes from above, from him.

So he says, “If you take away from yourself the bond, and the stretching out of the hand” (Isaiah 58:9). By “bond,” I think, he means wickedness of character, perversity and love of quarrels, and, as it were, tying knots of trouble against people and searching out crooked schemes, so as at times to bind people fast and throw them into snares of hardship from which there is no escape.

For a person must be straightforward and easy to approach, if he aims to be watched over by God and longs for the gifts that come from him. And by “the stretching out of the hand” he perhaps means taking bribes and reaching after shameful gain; for we sometimes say …
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 70, Commentary on Isaiah (CPG 5203). The section opens on the end of a word (…της) that completes φαιδρό… at the close of the previous section (‘the brightness of the saints’), and it ends mid-sentence (φαμὲν γὰρ ἔσθ’ ὅτε …).
[ἴσ. τῆς] is the editor’s suggestion to read τοῖς τῆς δικαιοσύνης ἐπιμεληταῖς, ‘those who devote themselves to righteousness’; the English follows it.
Psalm 34:15 is Psalm 33:16 and Psalm 18:6 is Psalm 17:7 in the Septuagint. Proverbs 15:29 follows the Septuagint (εὐχαῖς δὲ δικαίων ἐπακούει).
χειροτονία in the Septuagint of Isaiah 58:9 is ‘the stretching out of the hand’ (the Hebrew has ‘the pointing of the finger’); Cyril reads it as the hand held out for bribes.
τὴν τῶν ἐθνῶν μοχθηρίαν: ‘of the nations’ makes no sense in an address to the one who must put away the bond from himself; it is read as τῶν ἠθῶν, ‘wickedness of character’.
Column marker 70.1292 and the quotation markers 6 and lemma markers 9 are editorial and omitted.

title: Christ the Everlasting Light
english: … but we await new heavens and a new earth, and his promises, as it is written (2 Peter 3:13). The Savior himself said something of the same kind: “In those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light” (Mark 13:24; compare Matthew 24:29). For the glory of the Savior itself will be enough to give the saints their light.

But so that the present words may seem in some way to follow the sense of the verses before them, we approve this interpretation and say that the present lines also signify something else. The light of the sun, and that of the moon as well, is useful and necessary to the eyes of the body. Yet at night the sun’s light is withdrawn, and by day the moon’s, for they take turns yielding the work of shining to each other.

But the divine and spiritual light, he says, which the Savior of all puts into the hearts of believers through the Holy Spirit and through those who know well how to lead others into the mysteries, will be unquenchable, unceasing, and always shining. So the mind of each person stands in need neither of sun nor of moon to be enlightened or to see. For the mind is not lit by light that the senses perceive. It is content instead with the guiding light that comes through the Holy Spirit, and with a brightness that lets it behold the glory of Christ and how great a likeness he bears to the One who begot him, a likeness of essence, of course, and also lets it know without straying the way of the best life.

The Savior, then, has become everlasting light for us, and he makes this plain to us when he says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and again, “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world” (John 9:5), and, “Whoever follows me will never walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12).

“And the days of your mourning will be fulfilled, and your people will all be righteous, and they will inherit the land forever, guarding the planting, the works of his hands, for glory. The fewest will become thousands, and the least a great nation. I, the Lord, will gather them in due season” (Isaiah 60:20–22).

Those who say that the time of the consummation is indicated by the light of the sun or the moon no longer working, but rather being withdrawn so that our Lord may become everlasting light, say that for those who mourn now, whom the Savior also says will be comforted (Matthew 5:4), there will be an end of mourning …
translator_notes: The section opens mid-word ('ης,'); the lost start of the clause is marked with a leading ellipsis rather than filled in. The δέ is kept as 'but' because the clause plainly contrasts with something lost.
The section ends mid-word ('τέλος ἔσται τοῦ πενθεῖν κατ…'); the broken 'κατ…' is not translated and the paragraph ends with an ellipsis.
Column/page markers '70.1348' and '481' and the quote markers '6' and lemma markers '9' are editorial and omitted.
τῇ τῶν ἀνόπιν ἐννοίᾳ: 'the sense of the verses before them' (ἀνόπιν = above, earlier); Cyril approves the literal-eschatological reading and then offers a second, spiritual one.
φησίν in 'the divine and spiritual light, he says' is the prophet's voice as Cyril reads the verse; kept as 'he says'.
νοητός rendered 'spiritual' (light known by the mind, as opposed to αἰσθητός 'perceived by the senses'); μυσταγωγεῖν 'lead others into the mysteries', i.e. teachers who initiate believers.
ἀνάβλεψιν: 'to see' (recovery of sight / looking up); a narrower 'recovery of sight' would overstate a healing image here.

οὐσιωδῶς δὲ δηλονότι qualifies the Son's likeness (ἐμφέρεια) to the Father who begot him: 'a likeness of essence, of course'. Doctrinal point kept explicit: the likeness is in essence, not mere resemblance. 'The One who begot him' is capitalised because it names the Father.
κατὰ καιροὺς in the lemma: 'in due season'.
The final sentence reports other interpreters (Οἱ … λέγοντες … φασίν); it is kept as their view, not Cyril's own.
baehrens: PG 70 In Is. book5-part2 rem mid

title: God’s Anger and Our Sin
english: … shows his gentleness, unexpectedly saving those who have slipped away from every hope, and holding out a saving hand to those who are down low and lying, as it were, on the ground. Those who offer up the prayer before us say something like this: “From the foundation of the world we have neither heard of nor seen any such God, except you, and you alone” (compare Isaiah 64:4).

For to those who wait for you, that is, to those who have set their hope on you, he lavishes his mercy. For it will surely follow those who work righteousness, and it will be fitting for those to receive it who keep your ways in memory, that is, who carry out your will (compare Isaiah 64:4–5). For we say that the ways of the Lord are his commandments. So the inspired David sings at one time, “In your way I shall live” (compare Psalm 119:37), and at another, “I ran the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Psalm 119:32).

Tomos 6. “See, you were angry, and we sinned. Therefore we went astray, and we all became like the unclean, and all our righteousness like the rag of a woman in her impurity. We fell away like leaves because of our lawless deeds; so the wind will carry us off like dust. There is no one who calls on your name, or who remembers to take hold of you; for you turned your face away from us and handed us over because of our sins” (Isaiah 64:5–7).

Some of the interpreters decided to approach these words with a different sense. They reverse the order of the words, or rather the force of the thoughts, so that the saying becomes: “See, we sinned, and you were angry.” For the divine anger, they say, did not become the cause of their offending; rather, because they had behaved outrageously, God was angry. They fear, naturally enough, that the divine wrath might somehow be thought to bring about sin.

But I think this must be said: it is no charge against the divine wrath that those who have come under it are unable to escape the assault of sin. For as long as the One who saves us takes delight in us, we rise far above sin, and, keeping firmly away from the filth that comes from wickedness, we are crowned with the glories of spiritual courage. But when we embitter the Giver of our strength and the Lord of our courage, we fall into weakness and help…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 70, Commentary on Isaiah (CPG 5203). The section opens on the end of a word (…ῆς γαληνότητος) and ends mid-word (ἀδραν…, ‘helplessness’), marked with ellipses.

The ‘prayer before us’ is Cyril’s paraphrase of Septuagint Isaiah 64:4–5 (64:3–4 in the Septuagint), so it is cited with ‘compare’. Isaiah verse numbers follow the English Bible; in the Septuagint the lemma is 64:4b–6.
‘In your way I shall live’ is Cyril’s form of Psalm 119:37 (Septuagint 118:37, ‘give me life in your way’); Psalm 119:32 is Septuagint 118:32.
The heading {ΤΟΜΟΣ Ϛ} is read as Tomos 6 (the encoded numeral is the stigma); it is kept where it stands, before the lemma.
ῥάκος ἀποκαθημένης: ‘the rag of a woman in her impurity’ (a woman set apart during menstruation).
The view that the order of ‘you were angry’ and ‘we sinned’ should be reversed belongs to other interpreters (φασί); Cyril answers it in the last paragraph.
Column marker 70.1400 and the quotation markers 6 and lemma markers 9 are editorial and omitted.
baehrens: PG 70 In Is. book5-part2 rem close
